newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak SPP-Gazprom deal said damaging to economy.
newsitem.headline: Slovak SPP-Gazprom deal said damaging to economy.

text.p: A planned joint venture between Slovak gas distributor SPP and Russia's Gazprom will severely harm the Slovak economy, an opposition economist said on Monday.
The joint-venture, which the Slovak side proposes to be owned 50-50, would focus on deliveries of Russian gas to clients in volumes above their current long-term contracts.

"The joint-venture ownership setup means that possible future Slovak profits from extra deliveries of gas will be lower by 50 percent," Mikulas Dzurinda, ex-minister of transport and a leading member of the opposition Christian-Democratic Movement (KDH) told journalists.
"I would call this rather a loss rather than profit," he added.

Slovensky Plynarensky Priemysel s.p. (SPP) General director Jan Ducky said operation of the joint-venture would not influence current delivery contracts. He said he did not expect "big" profits from the joint-venture operation as placing extra-gas deliveries to current clients has been problematic.
Dzurinda said he expected the Russians to exert pressure to conclude new contracts with the joint-venture instead of SPP when the current long-term contracts expire.
"I am also afraid that the SPP stake (in the joint-venture) will be soon sold to third, private subjects...linked either to SPP management or the Russian side," he said.
SPP has been included in the list of Slovak companies excluded from privatisation. Ducky is currently in Moscow for the joint-venture talks and was not available for comment.
SPP is one of the most profitable Slovak companies, with 1996 after-tax profit expected at some 8.862 billion crowns on revenues totalling around 48 billion crowns.
Most of its revenues come from transit fees on Russian gas to western Europe, which last year totalled around 80 billion cubic metres.
The pipeline, which began operation in April 1971, serves about 10 major consumers in central and western Europe.
Gazprom pays for the transfer by supplying about four billion cubic metres of gas to Slovak consumers, which covers about two-thirds of domestic annual consumption.
